summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a complex history of Crohn’s disease, multiple abdominal surgeries, short bowel syndrome, and PTSD was admitted for acute abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever, initially concerning for a Crohn’s flare. Imaging showed no bowel obstruction but revealed aspiration pneumonia in the right lung, which was treated with intravenous levofloxacin. She was managed conservatively for a paralytic ileus with an NG tube, which was later removed as bowel function improved. She tolerated a soft diet and transitioned to oral pain medications. A colonoscopy was performed by her preferred gastroenterologist, showing no strictures or significant inflammation, though the prep was suboptimal. Her anxiety and PTSD were addressed with restart of citalopram and PRN benzodiazepines. She was discharged home in stable condition on a short course of oral antibiotics, with instructions to taper analgesics and follow up with her primary and specialty providers.
problems: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomitus
